narration.heard: Markus has another question. If he pays much less in premiums than the death benefit, how can his family receive a larger covered payment? The answer starts with risk pooling. An insurer combines many exposures and spreads the financial burden of covered losses across the group. Marcus's own premiums are not the limit of a covered claim. The insurer owes the benefit according to the policy contract.

Think of many individual policies supporting one insurance operation. Premiums help fund its obligations alongside other financial resources. The policy is not simply a personal savings account that pays back only what Marcus put in. Pooling does not prevent death. Require identical premiums or erase uncertainty. People can have different coverage amounts and risk classifications. The insurer must still price its policies and manage its resources carefully.

Now connect pooling to the law of large numbers. A larger group of comparable, largely independent exposures tends to have more predictable, average loss experience. The keyword is average. A large pool may have more total claims than a small pool. The useful improvement is greater predictability in relative terms. It does not tell the insurer who will die or guarantee an exact number of claims.

Use an invented example. Suppose 1 ,000 people each have a 1 % annual probability of a death claim. 1 ,000 times 1 % gives 10 expected claims. Expected means an average across many possible outcomes. This year's count could be 8, 10, 12, or another number. These are teaching assumptions, not real mortality figures or a premium quote. No individual outcome is identified.

Pair one extra claim in two groups, with the same assumed 1 % probability. In a group of 100, moving from one claim to two changes the rate from 1 % to 2%. In a group of 10 ,000, moving from 100 claims to 101 changes the rate to 1 .01%. One extra claim has a smaller effect on the larger group's rate. This illustrates sensitivity. Not a guarantee. Shared events can still cause many claims together.

The make -up of the group matters too. Imagine an insurance offer at a standard price. People who know they have a greater chance of loss are especially eager to apply. That tendency is adverse selection. It can occur even when everyone answers truthfully. Underwriting helps the insurer evaluate applications and classify risk using permitted information and rules. It does not eliminate uncertainty. Remember the distinctions, pooling spreads financial risk. Large numbers improve group estimates. Adverse selection concerns who seeks coverage, now answer the eight lesson questions, and review any mistakes before finishing.
